 Workers in GTA need to make at least $27.60 to afford reasonable living standard, network says | CBC News Loaded Toronto Workers in GTA need to make at least $27.60 to afford reasonable living standard, network says
 Living wage in the area highest across Ontario, sitting at $9.65 more than current minimum wage. Living wage in the region highest across Ontario, $9.65 more than current minimum wage
 Eleanor Yuneun Park · CBC News · Posted: Nov 12, 2026 2:02 PM EST | Last Updated: 39 minutes ago Play Listen to this article Estimated 5 minutes The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Greater Toronto Area workers need to make an hourly wage of at least $27.60 to afford a reasonable standard of living — the highest living wage in Ontario. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press) Social Sharing
 People in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) need to make an hourly wage of at least $27.60 to afford a reasonable standard of living, according to the Ontario Living Wage Network (OLWN).
 That’s the highest living wage across Ontario. It’s also $9.65 higher than the province's current minimum wage that increased to $17.95 from $17.60 as of Oct. 1.
 A living wage is the hourly wage a person needs to make to cover basic living expenses. The lowest living wage this year is $21.15 in London-Elgin-Oxford but the non-profit OWLN says there is no region in the province where making minimum wage is enough to afford the cost of living. 
 "It’s a big impact on people that are earning minimum wage," says OWLN executive director Anne Coleman in an interview with CBC Toronto, adding that many people in that situation need to make tough choices.
 "Which bills do you pay? Are you able to provide healthy food for yourself and your family? Put gas in the car so that you can get to and from work or buy that monthly transit pass?" said Coleman.
 "People who are earning less than a living wage are having to make some really difficult decisions."
 Ontario minimum wage just increased by 35 cents, but advocates say it's not enough
 Why living alone is becoming increasingly unaffordable for Torontonians
 Increase small but widespread 
 Across the province, the average living wage increased by 1.6 per cent since 2025, in what the OLWN report describes as a "more modest increase" compared to the increase from 2024-2025. 
 The GTA’s average living wage this year increased by 40 cents, and Ottawa — the region with the highest wage jump at three per cent — saw an increase of 70 cents.
 Even though the increases vary from region to region, all 10 regions in the province saw their living wage rates rise, said the OLWN report.
 Higher minimum wage, better business 
 Coleman says that it’s important to continue increasing the minimum wage — but not only because it helps employees. 
 "Paying a living wage is also a great way to have a successful business," said Coleman. “It helps with workplace culture, but employers also see higher retention rates."
 "When people are in a community and they’re earning a living wage, that additional money above the minimum wage is going right back into the local economy and they are able to support local businesses."
 WATCH | Struggling to get by? Here’s why minimum wage doesn’t cover the cost of living : Struggling to get by? Here’s why minimum wage doesn’t cover the cost of living
 October 1 | Duration closed caption 2:26 Ontario’s minimum wage just went up by 35 cents to $17.95 an hour. Meanwhile, workers' advocates say a living wage in Toronto would actually hover around $27. So what accounts for the gap? As CBC's Kate McGillivray reports, it's the latest chapter in a debate has been raging in the province for decades over how to address poverty and balance the interests of businesses and workers. There are around 150 GTA employers that are certified as living wage employers, who go beyond what is legally required in terms of paying employees, says Coleman. 
 Owner Jeff McLeod’s JDavis Painting is one of them, and he says the decision to match living wage was an easy one because the "math is straightforward."
 "We had two really good, high-quality painters, who we thought were going to move into leadership positions in the company, leave within a few months of one another," McLeod told CBC Toronto.
 It took the business six to 12 months to recover from the cost it took for them to find and train new people, said McLeod.
 He said he also sees it as a way to attract highly skilled people for the company.
 "The clients we’re attracting are ones that want workers to care about the work, who truly take pride in their craft, show up, and are happy to be working where they are," said McLeod. 
 "And for us, happy painters lead to happy clients."

 ﻿
 What makes a living wage, and why that matters for workers across Ontario 
 But Simon Gaudreault, chief economist at the Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses, says it isn't very realistic for many small and medium-sized businesses to offer a living wage.
 Many of the minimum-wage positions are entry-level jobs, he says, adding that they "require a lower skill level." 
 "Productivity is relatively low in that position, and that's why they're offering minimum wage in those positions with the hope of keeping those employees and training them," said Gaudreault in an interview with CBC Toronto. 
 The cost of training employees in entry-level jobs is also mostly done in-house and small business owners do not receive tax credit for informal training they provide, according to Gaudreault. 
 "That's why you need to strike the right balance between minimum wage and a market wage."

 Calculation method 
 OLWN calculates the living wage based on the before-tax amount that people in three types of households would need for a basket of goods and services when working 35 hours weekly. 
 The network divides the three types of households into a single adult, a single parent with a seven-year old, and two parents aged 35 with two children aged seven and three.
 The rate is based on a weighted average of the three family types, using 2021 census data.
 The basket of goods and services include food, shelter, clothing and footwear, and transportation, as well as a four per cent contingency amount for emergencies.
